Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, let
$C:=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] (c) when $\gamma>0$, and the free Fourier multiplier when $\gamma=0$,
and let $U$ be the unitary of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-angular-radial-unitary-reduction]] from $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$
onto $K=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^2\bigl((0,\infty),dr\bigr)$, with coefficients
$u_{lm}=r\,c_{lm}$. For $l\ge0$ let $V_l$ be the closure of
$C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$ in $L^2(0,\infty;\mathbb C)$ for the norm
$$\|u\|_{V_l}^2:=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\Bigl|u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr|^2+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}|u(r)|^2+|u(r)|^2\Bigr)dr,$$
realized as the space of $u\in L^2$ with $u'-\frac ur\in L^2$ and
$\int|u|^2/r^2<\infty$ in the distributional sense
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and define
$$a_l(u,v):=\int_0^\infty\Bigl[\overline{\Bigl(v'(r)-\frac{v(r)}{r}\Bigr)}\Bigl(u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr)+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u(r)\overline{v(r)}-\frac{\gamma}{r}u(r)\overline{v(r)}\Bigr]dr .$$
Then:

(a) $V_l$ is a dense linear subspace of $L^2(0,\infty)$ that is a Hilbert space for $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$, the inclusion $V_l\hookrightarrow L^2(0,\infty)$ is continuous, and $a_l$ is a bounded symmetric sesquilinear form on $V_l$ that is closed and semibounded below;

(b) the operator $A_l$ defined by
$$D(A_l):=\Bigl\{u\in V_l:\exists\,f\in L^2(0,\infty)\ \text{with}\ a_l(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle\ \forall v\in V_l\Bigr\},\qquad A_lu:=f,$$
is well defined, self-adjoint and bounded below; $D(A_l)$ is dense in $V_l$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$ and $a_l(u,u)=\langle A_lu,u\rangle$ for $u\in D(A_l)$;

(c) for every $u\in D(A_l)$ the distributional identity $-u''+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)u=A_lu$ holds on $(0,\infty)$; consequently $u\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(0,\infty)$, $u$ is of class $C^1$ with $u'$ locally absolutely continuous, and the identity holds pointwise almost everywhere on $(0,\infty)$; if moreover $A_lu=Eu$ for some constant $E\in\mathbb C$ (in particular if $u$ is an eigenfunction of $A_l$), then $u$ is of class $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ and the differential equation holds pointwise there;

(d) *block identity.* For $\psi\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with $U\psi=(u_{lm})$ one has $\psi\in D(C)$ if and only if $u_{lm}\in D(A_l)$ for every $(l,m)$ and $\sum_{l,m}\bigl(\|u_{lm}\|^2+\|A_lu_{lm}\|^2\bigr)<\infty$; then $U(C\psi)=(A_lu_{lm})_{l,m}$. Equivalently $UCU^*=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}A_l$ on $K$;

(e) *eigenfunction transport.* If $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=Eu$ for some $E\in\mathbb R$, then the function $\psi(x):=u(r)Y_{l0}(\Omega)/r$ (with $x=r\Omega$) lies in $H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, satisfies $C\psi=E\psi$, and $r\mapsto u(r)/r$ is bounded on $(0,1]$; moreover $\psi$ is bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R^3$.

No endpoint boundary condition is imposed by hand: the domain $D(A_l)$ is the
form-domain realization transported from $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and no
physical interpretation of $A_l$, $C$, $U$ or $\gamma$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<L<\infty$ and let
$V\in C([0,L];\mathbb C)$ with $M:=\|V\|_{C^0}=\max_{[0,L]}|V|$. For
$z\in\mathbb C$, $x_0\in[0,L]$ and $c_0,c_1\in\mathbb C$ consider the
initial value problem
$\text{(IVP)}\qquad -u''+Vu=zu,\qquad u(x_0)=c_0,\quad u'(x_0)=c_1,$
for $u\in C^2([0,L];\mathbb C)$. Then:

(a) (IVP) has exactly one solution $u(\cdot\,;z,x_0,c_0,c_1)$; it is the
unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$u(x)=c_0+c_1(x-x_0)+\int_{x_0}^x(x-t)\bigl(V(t)-z\bigr)u(t)\,dt
\qquad(x\in[0,L]),$
the integral over $[x_0,x]$ for $x<x_0$ carrying the negative orientation, and
$\sup_{[0,L]}|u|\le\bigl(|c_0|+|c_1|L\bigr)e^{(M+|z|)L^2};$

(b) for fixed $x_0,c_0,c_1$, put $p(x):=c_0+c_1(x-x_0)$ and, for
$f\in C([0,L];\mathbb C)$, define
$\mathcal K_zf(x):=\int_{x_0}^x(x-t)(V(t)-z)f(t)\,dt$. Then
$$u(x;z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(\mathcal K_z^np)(x)$$
and the termwise $x$-derivative series converge uniformly on
$[0,L]\times\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le R\}$ for every $R>0$. In particular,
$(x,z)\mapsto(u(x;z),u'(x;z))$ is continuous, and for each fixed $x$ both
$u(x;\cdot)$ and $u'(x;\cdot)$ are entire functions of $z$. The derivative
$w:=\partial_zu(\cdot\,;z)$ is the unique $C^2$ solution on $[0,L]$ of
$-w''+Vw-zw=u(\cdot\,;z),\qquad w(x_0)=0,\quad w'(x_0)=0 .$
It satisfies the associated Volterra equation
$w(x)=\int_{x_0}^x(x-t)\bigl[(V(t)-z)w(t)-u(t)\bigr]dt$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$, let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]), and let
$(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,\,-l\le m\le l}$ be the complete orthonormal family of
$L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]]. For pointwise formulas use the representatives $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]], and write $Y_{lm}(\Omega)$ for their values. Explicitly, with $P_l$ and $b_{lm}$ as in that supplier, for $0\le m\le l$,
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\Omega)=\frac{(-1)^m b_{lm}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2)^m P_l^{(m)}(\Omega_3),\qquad \widetilde Y_{l,-m}=(-1)^m\overline{\widetilde Y_{lm}}\quad(1\le m\le l).$$
These are restrictions of polynomials in the Cartesian coordinates, hence smooth on the entire sphere, and represent the stated $L^2$ classes. Write
$L^2=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with Lebesgue measure and inner product linear
in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-hilbert-space]]), and let
$$K:=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^2\bigl((0,\infty),dr;\mathbb C\bigr)$$
be the Hilbert direct sum over $l\ge0$, $-l\le m\le l$. For $\psi\in L^2$ and
each $(l,m)$ define the coefficient function and the reduced function
$$c_{lm}(r):=\int_{S^2}\psi(r\Omega)\overline{Y_{lm}(\Omega)}\,d\sigma(\Omega)\quad(r>0,\ \text{a.e.}),\qquad u_{lm}(r):=r\,c_{lm}(r).$$
Then:

(a) for every $\psi\in L^2$ and every $(l,m)$ the function $u_{lm}$ is a well-defined element of $L^2((0,\infty),dr)$ depending only on the class of $\psi$, and $U\psi:=(u_{lm})_{l,m}$ is a linear isometry of $L^2$ into (indeed onto) $K$ with
$$\|U\psi\|_K^2=\sum_{l\ge0}\sum_{m=-l}^{l}\int_0^\infty|u_{lm}(r)|^2\,dr=\|\psi\|_{L^2}^2;$$

(b) $U$ is unitary, and for every $(u_{lm})\in K$ the finite-subset sums $\sum_{l\le N,\,|m|\le l}u_{lm}(r)Y_{lm}(\Omega)/r$ converge in $L^2$ to a function $\psi$ with $U\psi=(u_{lm})$;

(c) on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ every $f\in C^2$ satisfies the following identity. Here radial derivatives differentiate $F(r,\Omega)=f(r\Omega)$ with $\Omega$ fixed, and in angle coordinates $\Delta_{S^2}F:=\partial_\theta^2F+\cot\theta\,\partial_\theta F+\sin^{-2}\theta\,\partial_\varphi^2F$, extended continuously to the poles by the Cartesian identity proved below. For the smooth representatives of $Y_{lm}$ this agrees with the negative of the diagonal sphere operator in [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]]:

$$\Delta f=\partial_r^2f+\frac2r\partial_rf+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{S^2}f;$$

(d) for every $l\ge0$, $m$, and $u\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$, the function $\psi:=u(r)Y_{lm}(\Omega)/r$ lies in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\subseteq H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, its image under $U$ is the finite-support vector with $(l,m)$-entry $u$, and
$$-\Delta\psi=\frac1r\Bigl(-u''(r)+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u(r)\Bigr)Y_{lm}(\Omega),\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla\psi|^2\,dx=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\Bigl|u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr|^2+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}|u(r)|^2\Bigr)dr .$$

All statements are purely mathematical assertions about $L^2$ spaces, the
surface measure and the Laplacian; no physical interpretation and no statement
about operators with unbounded potentials is included.

Let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le n$. Then, in $\mathbb{N}$,

$$\binom{n}{k}\cdot k!\cdot (n-k)! = n! ,$$

and consequently:

1. $\binom{n}{k}\cdot k! = n^{\underline{k}}$
   ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]);
2. **integrality**: in $\mathbb{R}$,
   $\iota\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{\iota(n!)}{\iota(k!)\,\iota((n-k)!)}$, so the
   familiar quotient $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$ is the canonical natural of a natural
   number, namely of the count $\binom{n}{k}$;
3. **symmetry**: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$.

Here $\iota$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]] and $n-k$ the
truncated difference, which for $k \le n$ is the ordinary one.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]), let $S$ be a finite set with $n:=|S|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and let $a:S\to M$. Choose a bijection $\phi:n\to S$ and define

$$\sum_{s\in S}a_s:=a_{\phi(0)}+a_{\phi(1)}+\cdots+a_{\phi(n-1)},$$

where the right side is the finite monoid product of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] written additively. In particular, the sum over the empty set is $0$.

This value is independent of the enumeration. If $\psi:n\to S$ is another bijection, then $\phi^{-1}\circ\psi$ is a permutation of $n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and generalised commutativity gives

$$\sum_{k<n}a_{\psi(k)}=\sum_{k<n}a_{\phi(k)}$$

([[thm-generalised-associativity]]). Thus the displayed notation names one element of $M$ and does not select a preferred enumeration.

When $M$ is the additive monoid of $\mathbb R$ or of $\mathbb N$, this definition agrees with [[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]: both enumerate $S$, apply the same finite recursion with identity $0$, and are independent of the enumeration.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

derivations.claim: [Substitution without dividing by a solution] Put $h(r)=r^{l+1}e^{-kr}$ and $u=h\varphi$. The multiplier $h$ is smooth and nonzero for every $r>0$, so $u\leftrightarrow\varphi$ preserves $C^2$. Its derivatives satisfy $h'/h=(l+1)/r-k$ and $h''/h=l(l+1)/r^2-2k(l+1)/r+k^2$. The product rule gives the identity $-u''+[l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r+k^2]u=-h[\varphi''+(2(l+1)/r-2k)\varphi'+(\gamma-2k(l+1))\varphi/r]$. Therefore the radial equation is equivalent to $r\varphi''+(2l+2-2kr)\varphi'+(\gamma-2k(l+1))\varphi=0$. Write $\varphi(r)=\widetilde v(2kr)$: then $\varphi'=2k\widetilde v'$ and $\varphi''=(2k)^2\widetilde v''$, and division by the nonzero scalar $2k$ gives $x\widetilde v''+(2l+2-x)\widetilde v'+j\widetilde v=0$. The Statement's $v(x)=e^{x/2}x^{-(l+1)}u(x/(2k))$ equals $(2k)^{-(l+1)}\widetilde v(x)$; multiplication by this constant preserves the homogeneous equation. All transformations are reversible, including at zeros of $u$, and establish (a).

[Convergence with every differentiated series] Let $b=2l+2$ and $B=\max\{1,|j|/b\}$. The recurrence gives $|v_{i+1}|\le B|v_i|/(i+1)$ because $i+|j|\le B(i+b)$. Induction from $v_0=1$ yields $|v_i|\le B^i/i!$. For any derivative order $q\ge0$ and $R>0$, the $q$-th formal derivative on $|x|\le R$ has absolute sum bounded by $\sum_{i\ge q}B^iR^{i-q}/(i-q)!=B^qe^{BR}$. Every differentiated series therefore converges uniformly on that compact interval. To justify differentiation explicitly, integrate the uniformly convergent first derivative series from $0$ to $x$; the integral of its finite partial sums is the corresponding original partial sum minus its value at zero, and uniform convergence allows passage to the limit. The fundamental theorem for a continuous integrand proves the derivative identity. Repeating this for successive derivative series proves $v\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with all asserted derivatives.

[Coefficient equation] By step 1.2, substitution and collection of coefficients are legitimate. The coefficient of $x^i$ in $xv''+bv'-xv'+jv$ is $(i+1)(i+b)v_{i+1}+(j-i)v_i$ for each $i\ge0$, including $i=0$ because the $xv''$ contribution then vanishes. The recurrence makes every coefficient zero; the equation thus holds for all real $x$. Conversely this same coefficient comparison shows that an analytic solution with constant coefficient $1$ must have exactly this recurrence. This proves (b).

[Exact termination and polynomial normalization] If $j\notin\mathbb N_0$, every factor $i-j$ is nonzero, so all $v_i$ are nonzero. Such a series cannot be a polynomial: its $i$-th derivative at zero is $i!v_i$ by step 1.2. If $j=n\in\mathbb N_0$, the coefficients through $v_n$ are nonzero, $v_{n+1}=0$, and the recurrence forces all later coefficients to vanish. For the stated Laguerre polynomial, $c_i=(-1)^i\binom{n+a}{n-i}/i!$ has $c_0\ne0$ and $c_{i+1}/c_i=(i-n)/[(i+1)(a+i+1)]$ for $0\le i<n$, by the factorial identities in [F4]. Since $a+i+1=i+2l+2$, it has precisely the same recurrence and $v=L_n^{(2l+1)}/\binom{n+2l+1}{n}$. Its leading coefficient is nonzero. Thus the polynomial and nonzero normalization claims in (d) follow.

[The regular branch and a zero-free initial interval] The function $u_1=u_{\mathrm{reg}}=r^{l+1}e^{-kr}v(2kr)$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$ and solves the radial equation by steps 1.1 and 2.1. Since $v(0)=1$ and $v$ is smooth, $u_1=r^{l+1}(1+O(r))$ as $r\downarrow0$. It is real valued because the recurrence has real coefficients. Choose $\delta>0$ so that $u_1(r)/r^{l+1}>1/2$ throughout $(0,\delta)$. Hence $u_1$ has no zero there and has the required normalized endpoint limit.

[Local second solution and its exact leading asymptotic] Fix $r_*\in(0,\delta)$, put $I(r)=\int_{r_*}^ru_1(s)^{-2}ds$, and define $u_2=u_1I$ only on $(0,\delta)$. Here $I'=u_1^{-2}$, so $u_2'=u_1'I+u_1^{-1}$, $u_2''=u_1''I$, and $W(u_1,u_2):=u_1u_2'-u_1'u_2=1$. Thus $u_2$ solves the same equation and is independent of $u_1$. Set $p=2l+1>0$. Since $u_1(s)^{-2}/s^{-p-1}\to1$, comparison between $(1-\eta)s^{-p-1}$ and $(1+\eta)s^{-p-1}$ below any sufficiently small fixed endpoint shows $r^p\int_r^{r_*}u_1(s)^{-2}ds\to1/p$: the integral above that endpoint is finite and disappears after multiplication by $r^p$, while $r^p\int_r^ts^{-p-1}ds=(1-(r/t)^p)/p$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ gives $I(r)\sim-r^{-p}/p$, hence $u_2(r)\sim-r^{-l}/(2l+1)$. In particular $|u_2|/r\to\infty$ and $|u_2|/r^{l+1}\to\infty$, also when $l=0$.

[Integrability and actual form-domain approximation] Suppose $j\in\mathbb N_0$. By step 3.1, $u=u_1$ is a polynomial times $r^{l+1}e^{-kr}$. Near zero $u=O(r^{l+1})$, $u'=O(r^l)$, $u/r=O(r^l)$; at infinity each is bounded by an exponential times a polynomial. Their squared integrals are finite: on $(0,1)$ compare with $r^{2l}$, while at infinity a polynomial times $e^{-2kr}$ is integrable, as follows by bounding each power using the exponential series or repeated integration by parts. Thus $u,u',u/r\in L^2$, and $u$ has zero trace at zero. To show membership in the actual completion $V_l$, take smooth cutoffs $\eta_\varepsilon$ vanishing below $\varepsilon$, equal to one above $2\varepsilon$, with $|\eta_\varepsilon'|\le K/\varepsilon$, and $\chi_R$ equal to one below $R$, vanishing above $2R$, with $|\chi_R'|\le K/R$. The products $u_{\varepsilon,R}=\eta_\varepsilon\chi_Ru$ lie in $C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$. The omitted $L^2$, derivative and $u/r$ tails tend to zero; the added derivative at zero obeys $\|\eta_\varepsilon'u\|_2^2\le4K^2\int_0^{2\varepsilon}|u/r|^2dr\to0$, and the added derivative at infinity obeys $\|\chi_R'u\|_2^2\le K^2R^{-2}\int_R^{2R}|u|^2dr\to0$. Hence $u_{\varepsilon,R}\to u$ in $V_l$, for instance along $\varepsilon=1/n$, $R=n$. This proves (d)'s $L^2$ claim and establishes $u\in V_l$.

[Global continuation across every node] Put $q(r)=l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r+k^2$, continuous on $(0,\infty)$. For $n\ge1$ let $J_n=[r_*/(n+1),(n+1)r_*]$. Apply [F2] on each $J_n$ to $u''=qu$ with initial data $u_2(r_*)=0$, $u_2'(r_*)=u_1(r_*)^{-1}$. The unique solutions agree on nested overlaps and with step 4.1 wherever the latter is defined, so their union is a $C^2$ solution on $\bigcup_nJ_n=(0,\infty)$. No blowup at a finite positive node is possible because every such node lies inside one regular compact IVP interval. Differentiating the Wronskian gives $W'=u_1u_2''-u_1''u_2=0$, and its value at $r_*$ is $1$, so $W=1$ globally. If $u_1(t)=0$, then $-u_1'(t)u_2(t)=1$; this also shows that every such node is simple and the continued $u_2$ is finite and nonzero there. The reciprocal integral of step 4.1 is never used across a node.

[Form eigenidentity and the full operator domain] For $w\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$ expand the kinetic integrand: $(u'-u/r)\overline{(w'-w/r)}=u'\overline{w'}-u'\overline w/r-u\overline{w'}/r+u\overline w/r^2$. The last three terms are $-(u\overline w/r)'$ and have zero integral because $w$ is compactly supported away from the endpoints. Therefore $a_l(u,w)=\int[u'\overline{w'}+l(l+1)u\overline w/r^2-\gamma u\overline w/r]=\int[-u''+(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r)u]\overline w=-k^2\langle u,w\rangle$. Compact tests are dense in $V_l$ by its definition, $a_l$ is bounded by [F1], and $w\mapsto\langle u,w\rangle$ is continuous in its norm. The identity extends to every $w\in V_l$. The defining condition in [F1] gives $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=-k^2u$. For every allowed $m$, the family with sole nonzero $(l,m)$ entry $u$ has finite graph norm; the exact block identity gives $\psi=uY_{lm}/r\in D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ and $C\psi=-k^2\psi$. Conversely that single-block domain identity gives the stated equivalence. This establishes (e).

[Arbitrary solutions and endpoint uniqueness] At $r_*$ the initial-data matrix with columns $(u_1,u_1')$ and $(u_2,u_2')$ has determinant $1$ by step 5.1. For any solution $u$, solve the invertible two-by-two linear system for $c_1,c_2\in\mathbb C$ matching $(u(r_*),u'(r_*))$. The IVP uniqueness of [F2] on the nested $J_n$ gives $u=c_1u_1+c_2u_2$ everywhere. If $c_2\ne0$, the asymptotics in steps 3.2 and 4.1 give $u(r)\sim-c_2r^{-l}/(2l+1)$, since $u_1/u_2\to0$. Hence $|u|/r\to\infty$ and $|u|/r^{l+1}\to\infty$. If $c_2=0$, the latter ratio is bounded, and every nonzero such solution is a nonzero scalar multiple of $u_1$. This proves all of (c); the zero solution is included in the general linear representation.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<L<\infty$ and let
$V\in C([0,L];\mathbb C)$ with $M:=\|V\|_{C^0}=\max_{[0,L]}|V|$. For
$z\in\mathbb C$, $x_0\in[0,L]$ and $c_0,c_1\in\mathbb C$ consider the
initial value problem
$\text{(IVP)}\qquad -u''+Vu=zu,\qquad u(x_0)=c_0,\quad u'(x_0)=c_1,$
for $u\in C^2([0,L];\mathbb C)$. Then:

(a) (IVP) has exactly one solution $u(\cdot\,;z,x_0,c_0,c_1)$; it is the
unique continuous solution of the Volterra equation
$u(x)=c_0+c_1(x-x_0)+\int_{x_0}^x(x-t)\bigl(V(t)-z\bigr)u(t)\,dt
\qquad(x\in[0,L]),$
the integral over $[x_0,x]$ for $x<x_0$ carrying the negative orientation, and
$\sup_{[0,L]}|u|\le\bigl(|c_0|+|c_1|L\bigr)e^{(M+|z|)L^2};$

(b) for fixed $x_0,c_0,c_1$, put $p(x):=c_0+c_1(x-x_0)$ and, for
$f\in C([0,L];\mathbb C)$, define
$\mathcal K_zf(x):=\int_{x_0}^x(x-t)(V(t)-z)f(t)\,dt$. Then
$$u(x;z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(\mathcal K_z^np)(x)$$
and the termwise $x$-derivative series converge uniformly on
$[0,L]\times\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le R\}$ for every $R>0$. In particular,
$(x,z)\mapsto(u(x;z),u'(x;z))$ is continuous, and for each fixed $x$ both
$u(x;\cdot)$ and $u'(x;\cdot)$ are entire functions of $z$. The derivative
$w:=\partial_zu(\cdot\,;z)$ is the unique $C^2$ solution on $[0,L]$ of
$-w''+Vw-zw=u(\cdot\,;z),\qquad w(x_0)=0,\quad w'(x_0)=0 .$
It satisfies the associated Volterra equation
$w(x)=\int_{x_0}^x(x-t)\bigl[(V(t)-z)w(t)-u(t)\bigr]dt$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

The functions $\sin,\cos,\sinh,\cosh$ are entire and satisfy
$$\sin'=\cos,\qquad \cos'=-\sin,\qquad \sinh'=\cosh,\qquad \cosh'=\sinh.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, let
$C:=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] (c) when $\gamma>0$, and the free Fourier multiplier when $\gamma=0$,
and let $U$ be the unitary of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-angular-radial-unitary-reduction]] from $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$
onto $K=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^2\bigl((0,\infty),dr\bigr)$, with coefficients
$u_{lm}=r\,c_{lm}$. For $l\ge0$ let $V_l$ be the closure of
$C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$ in $L^2(0,\infty;\mathbb C)$ for the norm
$$\|u\|_{V_l}^2:=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\Bigl|u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr|^2+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}|u(r)|^2+|u(r)|^2\Bigr)dr,$$
realized as the space of $u\in L^2$ with $u'-\frac ur\in L^2$ and
$\int|u|^2/r^2<\infty$ in the distributional sense
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and define
$$a_l(u,v):=\int_0^\infty\Bigl[\overline{\Bigl(v'(r)-\frac{v(r)}{r}\Bigr)}\Bigl(u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr)+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u(r)\overline{v(r)}-\frac{\gamma}{r}u(r)\overline{v(r)}\Bigr]dr .$$
Then:

(a) $V_l$ is a dense linear subspace of $L^2(0,\infty)$ that is a Hilbert space for $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$, the inclusion $V_l\hookrightarrow L^2(0,\infty)$ is continuous, and $a_l$ is a bounded symmetric sesquilinear form on $V_l$ that is closed and semibounded below;

(b) the operator $A_l$ defined by
$$D(A_l):=\Bigl\{u\in V_l:\exists\,f\in L^2(0,\infty)\ \text{with}\ a_l(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle\ \forall v\in V_l\Bigr\},\qquad A_lu:=f,$$
is well defined, self-adjoint and bounded below; $D(A_l)$ is dense in $V_l$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$ and $a_l(u,u)=\langle A_lu,u\rangle$ for $u\in D(A_l)$;

(c) for every $u\in D(A_l)$ the distributional identity $-u''+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)u=A_lu$ holds on $(0,\infty)$; consequently $u\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(0,\infty)$, $u$ is of class $C^1$ with $u'$ locally absolutely continuous, and the identity holds pointwise almost everywhere on $(0,\infty)$; if moreover $A_lu=Eu$ for some constant $E\in\mathbb C$ (in particular if $u$ is an eigenfunction of $A_l$), then $u$ is of class $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ and the differential equation holds pointwise there;

(d) *block identity.* For $\psi\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with $U\psi=(u_{lm})$ one has $\psi\in D(C)$ if and only if $u_{lm}\in D(A_l)$ for every $(l,m)$ and $\sum_{l,m}\bigl(\|u_{lm}\|^2+\|A_lu_{lm}\|^2\bigr)<\infty$; then $U(C\psi)=(A_lu_{lm})_{l,m}$. Equivalently $UCU^*=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}A_l$ on $K$;

(e) *eigenfunction transport.* If $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=Eu$ for some $E\in\mathbb R$, then the function $\psi(x):=u(r)Y_{l0}(\Omega)/r$ (with $x=r\Omega$) lies in $H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, satisfies $C\psi=E\psi$, and $r\mapsto u(r)/r$ is bounded on $(0,1]$; moreover $\psi$ is bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R^3$.

No endpoint boundary condition is imposed by hand: the domain $D(A_l)$ is the
form-domain realization transported from $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and no
physical interpretation of $A_l$, $C$, $U$ or $\gamma$ is asserted.

A continuous function on an open subset of $\mathbb C$ is holomorphic if and only if its integral around the boundary of every filled triangle contained in the open set is zero.

Precisely, if $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ is open and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is continuous, then

$$f\text{ is holomorphic on }\Omega\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\int_{\partial\Delta[a,b,c]}f(z)\,dz=0\text{ whenever }\Delta[a,b,c]\subseteq\Omega.$$

Repeated or collinear vertices are permitted.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and let $g_j:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Suppose the sequence of partial sums of $\sum_{j\ge0}g_j$ converges locally uniformly to $g$. Then $g$ is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$,

$$g^{(k)}=\sum_{j\ge0}g_j^{(k)},$$

where the derivative series converges locally uniformly.

derivations.claim: [Regular solution] On a compact $k$-set choose $C\ge\max(1,\gamma,\sup|k|)$. Induction gives $|c_n|\le C^n/n!$, since the recurrence majorant divided by $C^n/n!$ is $[\gamma/C+|k|^2(n-1)/C^2]/(n+2l+1)\le1$; at $n=1$ the second term is absent. Each $c_n$ is a polynomial in $k^2$. The exponential majorant also bounds every fixed $r$-derivative on compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$, so the series is entire in $k$, smooth in $r>0$, and termwise substitution gives the stated radial equation. Its leading coefficient is one, and the remaining series tends to zero as $r\downarrow0$, uniformly on compact $k$-sets. For real $k$ all coefficients and $\varphi_l$ are real.

[A common tail and the correct complex-power modulus] Perform the construction on $\mathcal D:=\{\operatorname{Re}k>0,\operatorname{Im}k\ge0\}$, then restrict to $K$. Fix a compact $Q\subset\mathcal D$, and put $m:=\min_Q|k|>0$, $A:=\max_Q|a|$, $B:=\max_Q|b|$, $H:=2/m+2A/m^2$, and $D:=BH$. Choose $r_0\ge\max(1,\gamma/(2m^2),2A/m,2D)$. For $s\ge y\ge r_0$, the exact modulus is $|w(s)^2w(y)^{-2}|=\exp[-2\operatorname{Im}k(s-y)](s/y)^{-2\operatorname{Im}a}$. Here $-2\operatorname{Im}a=\gamma\operatorname{Im}k/|k|^2$, and $\log(s/y)\le(s-y)/y$ makes this modulus at most one. Write $p(y)=k+a/y$ and $d(y)=1/(-2ip(y))$. Then $|p|\ge m/2$, $|d|\le1/m$ and $|d'|\le2A/(m^2y^2)$. Integration by parts on the finite interval gives $w(s)^2\int_r^s w(y)^{-2}dy=d(s)-d(r)w(s)^2w(r)^{-2}-\int_r^s d'(y)w(s)^2w(y)^{-2}dy$, whose modulus is at most $H$. Thus the actual kernel $R(k;r,s):=b s^{-2}w(s)^2\int_r^s w(y)^{-2}dy$ satisfies $|R|\le D/s^2$, uniformly for $k\in Q$ and $s\ge r\ge r_0$.

[Contraction and bounded-solution uniqueness] On the complete space $C_b([r_0,\infty);\mathbb C)$ define $(\mathcal V_k h)(r)=\int_r^\infty R(k;r,s)h(s)ds$. The kernel estimate gives $\|\mathcal V_k\|\le D/r_0\le1/2$; continuity follows by splitting the integral at a finite upper limit and using the uniformly small $s^{-2}$ tail. Therefore $v=\sum_{n\ge0}\mathcal V_k^n1$ is the unique fixed point of $h\mapsto1+\mathcal V_kh$, and $\|v\|_\infty\le2$, $|v(r)-1|\le2D/r$. Any bounded function for which the integral equation holds is continuous by the same kernel estimate and hence equals this fixed point. Constructions on different common tails agree on their overlap by uniqueness. This proves bounded-solution uniqueness on the chosen tail and the uniform $O(r^{-1})$ estimate.

[Differentiate the genuine double integral] In the integral equation the lower-limit term vanishes because $R(k;r,r)=0$, whereas $\partial_rR=-b s^{-2}w(s)^2w(r)^{-2}$. The ratio bound in step 1.2 dominates this derivative times $v(s)$ by $2B/s^2$ on each compact $r$-interval in the tail. Truncated-integral differentiation followed by uniform convergence therefore gives $v'(r)=-b w(r)^{-2}I(r)$, where $I(r):=\int_r^\infty w(s)^2v(s)s^{-2}ds$; this is a derivative identity, not a replacement of the original fixed-point equation by $v=1+bI$. The integral for $I$ is absolutely convergent: for real $k$, $|w|=1$, and for $\operatorname{Im}k>0$, $|w(s)|=e^{-\operatorname{Im}k s}s^{-\operatorname{Im}a}$ decays exponentially times a power. Hence $I'=-w(r)^2v(r)/r^2$ and $v''=-2i(k+a/r)v'+bv/r^2$. The ratio estimate gives $|v'|\le2B/r$, uniformly on $Q$. Using $w''=-[(k+a/r)^2+ia/r^2]w$ and $2ka=\gamma$, the product rule for $f=wv$ gives $f''=[-k^2-\gamma/r+l(l+1)/r^2]f$. Consequently $f=w[1+O(r^{-1})]$ and $f'=w[ik+O(r^{-1})]$, with the factor $w$ retained and all errors uniform on $Q$.

[Continuity and holomorphy on the common tail] Each Picard iterate is jointly continuous in $(k,r)$ on $Q\times[r_0,\infty)$: on compact $r$-intervals the finite-integral kernel is continuous, and the $D/s^2$ majorant makes the improper tail uniformly small. Induction on iterates followed by the uniform geometric bound $\|\mathcal V_k^n1\|_\infty\le2^{-n}$ proves joint continuity of $v$; the derivative formula, dominated by $2B/s^2$, also proves joint continuity of $v'$. On each triangle in $\{\operatorname{Re}k>0,\operatorname{Im}k>0\}$ with a compact neighborhood, the finite-integral kernel is holomorphic because $1/k$ and the complex exponential are holomorphic. If an iterate is holomorphic, interchange its $s$-integral with the triangle contour integral using the uniform $s^{-2}$ bound; the contour integral vanishes, so Morera proves that the next iterate is holomorphic. Uniform convergence and [F7] prove holomorphy of $v$. Apply the same contour argument to $v'=-\int_r^\infty b s^{-2}w(s)^2w(r)^{-2}v(s)ds$ to prove holomorphy of its initial data. Thus $f,f'$ are continuous to real $k$ and holomorphic in the open first quadrant. The construction on $\mathcal D$ also supplies an open complex neighborhood for points with $\operatorname{Re}k=k_{\min}$ and $\operatorname{Im}k>0$, which makes the asserted holomorphy at that boundary precise.

[First integration by parts improves the derivative] Fix real $k>0$ and write $Q(r)=2i\theta'(r)=2i(k+a/r)$ and $h(r)=v(r)/r^2$. Since $\theta'\ge k$, $Q^{-1}$ is bounded and its first two derivatives are $O(r^{-2})$ and $O(r^{-3})$. Initially $v=O(1)$ and $v'=O(r^{-1})$, so $h=O(r^{-2})$, $h'=O(r^{-3})$ and $(h/Q)'=O(r^{-3})$. Integration by parts, whose boundary term vanishes at infinity, gives $I(r)=-e^{2i\theta(r)}h(r)/Q(r)-\int_r^\infty e^{2i\theta(s)}(h/Q)'(s)ds=O(r^{-2})$. The exact derivative identity then gives $v'=O(r^{-2})$; the ODE from step 3.1 gives $v''=O(r^{-2})$.

[Extend to every positive radius] Fix $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than the common $r_0$. The regular-IVP result gives a unique extension of $f$ from $(f(r_0),f'(r_0))$ across $[\varepsilon,r_0]$. To establish complex parameter dependence rather than invoking that supplier's real-parameter differentiability clause, write $Y=(f,f')^{\mathsf T}$ and $Y'=M(k,r)Y$, with $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\ l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r-k^2&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Its initial-value integral series on $[\varepsilon,r_0]$ has $n$th term bounded by $C_0[C_M(r_0-\varepsilon)]^n/n!$, uniformly on compact $k$-sets, since the $n$fold ordered integration simplex has volume at most $(r_0-\varepsilon)^n/n!$. Each term is continuous to real $k$ and holomorphic in the open first quadrant by finite contour integration. Thus the sum has both properties by [F7], agrees with the unique IVP solution, and supplies the asserted parameter properties for every $r>0$. Set $v=f/w$ on the extension; $w$ never vanishes, so the same properties hold for $v$. Patching overlapping tails and intervals is unambiguous by IVP uniqueness. For fixed nonreal $k\in\mathcal D$, $f,f'$ have the stated exponential-times-power decay.

[Second integration gives the amplitude coefficient] Now $h''=v''/r^2-4v'/r^3+6v/r^4=O(r^{-4})$. Put $j=(h/Q)'$. Then $j=O(r^{-3})$, $j'=O(r^{-4})$ and $(j/Q)'=O(r^{-4})$. A second integration by parts gives $\int_r^\infty e^{2i\theta}j=-e^{2i\theta(r)}j(r)/Q(r)-\int_r^\infty e^{2i\theta}(j/Q)'=O(r^{-3})$. Therefore $I(r)=-e^{2i\theta(r)}v(r)/(2i\theta'(r)r^2)+O(r^{-3})$, $v'=bv/(2i\theta'r^2)+O(r^{-3})=b/(2ik r^2)+O(r^{-3})$, and integration to the known limit $v(\infty)=1$ gives $v=1-b/(2ik r)+O(r^{-2})$. Since $-b/(2ik)=-a/(2k)+i[a^2+l(l+1)]/(2k)$ and $|w|=1$, the coefficient is $|f|^2=|v|^2=1-a/(kr)+O(r^{-2})$. These estimates are uniform when real $k$ is restricted to a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$, because all preceding constants and the lower bound for $\theta'$ can be chosen uniformly.

[Real-energy Wronskians] Any real $k>0$ belongs to the public domain $\mathcal D$ of the single patched family $f_l$. By the asymptotic formulas, $W(\overline f,f)=2i(k+a/r)|v|^2+2i\operatorname{Im}(\overline vv')=2ik+O(r^{-1})$. It is constant by [F2], hence equals $2ik$. The pair $f,\overline f$ is therefore a basis of the two-dimensional solution space. If $W(\varphi_l,f)=0$, their initial data are proportional at any positive radius, hence IVP uniqueness implies $f=c\varphi_l$; neither solution is identically zero, by their normalizations. Since $\varphi_l$ is real, proportionality forces $W(\overline f,f)=0$, a contradiction. Thus $W_l(k)\ne0$, every solution is $Af+B\overline f$, and the nonzero $\varphi_l$ has such a representation with coefficients not both zero.

[The mixed term has a bounded integral] For fixed $R>r_0$, integration by parts gives $\int_R^L f^2=[e^{2i\theta}v^2/Q]_R^L-\int_R^L e^{2i\theta}(v^2/Q)'$. The endpoint term is uniformly bounded and $(v^2/Q)'=2vv'/Q+v^2(Q^{-1})'=O(r^{-2})$ is integrable, hence the whole integral is bounded independently of $L$. Expanding $|Af+B\overline f|^2=(|A|^2+|B|^2)|f|^2+2\operatorname{Re}(A\overline B f^2)$ and integrating step 5.2 yields $\int_R^L|Af+B\overline f|^2=(|A|^2+|B|^2)[L-R-(a/k)\log(L/R)]+O(1)$, with $a/k=\gamma/(2k^2)$. If at least one coefficient is nonzero the integral diverges, since its linear term dominates the logarithm; if both vanish it is zero. Every positive-energy eigenfunction in $D(A_l)$ is an $L^2$ classical solution by [F6], hence step 6.1 and this divergence exclude such an eigenfunction.

[Conclusion and choice accounting] Steps 1.1; 1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1; 6.1; and 4.2, 5.2 and 7.1 prove (a), (b), (c), and (d), respectively, for precisely the stated radial operator and parameter range. The explicit regular series, prescribed Picard iteration and unique IVP patching require no new arbitrary choice of solutions. The public Countable Choice assumption is retained for the invoked IVP and Hilbert-space suppliers; the public Axiom of Choice assumption is retained for the existing transported radial-operator supplier contract. No reduction of that supplier's choice hypothesis is inferred from this local argument.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, $l\ge0$,
$k>0$, let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]], write
$$j:=\frac{\gamma}{2k}-l-1,$$
and for $a=2l+1$ and $n\in\mathbb N_0$ let
$$L_n^{(a)}(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i\binom{n+a}{n-i}\frac{x^i}{i!}$$
be the $n$-th Laguerre polynomial of order $a$. Then:

(a) *substitution.* A $C^2$ function $u$ on $(0,\infty)$ satisfies $-u''+(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r)u=-k^2u$ if and only if $v(x):=e^{x/2}x^{-(l+1)}u(x/2k)$ is $C^2$ and satisfies $xv''+(2l+2-x)v'+jv=0$ on $(0,\infty)$;

(b) *regular series.* With $v_0:=1$ and
$$v_{i+1}:=\frac{(i-j)v_i}{(i+1)(i+2l+2)}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
the power series $v(x):=\sum_{i\ge0}v_ix^i$ converges for every $x\in\mathbb R$ and defines a solution of $xv''+(2l+2-x)v'+jv=0$ on $\mathbb R$;

(c) *regular solution and general solution.* The function
$$u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r):=r^{l+1}e^{-kr}v(2kr)$$
is a $C^\infty$ solution of the radial equation on $(0,\infty)$ with $u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)/r^{l+1}\to1$ as $r\downarrow0$; it is, up to a nonzero scalar multiple, the only solution with $u(r)/r^{l+1}$ bounded as $r\downarrow0$; every solution of the radial equation on $(0,\infty)$ is $c_1u_{\mathrm{reg}}+c_2u_2$ with $u_2$ defined near zero by $u_2(r):=u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)\int_{r_*}^r u_{\mathrm{reg}}(s)^{-2}ds$, where $0<r_*<\delta$ and $u_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has no zero in $(0,\delta)$, and extended uniquely to $(0,\infty)$ by the regular initial-value equation, and every solution that is not a multiple of $u_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has $|u(r)|/r$ unbounded as $r\downarrow0$;

(d) *termination.* $v$ is a polynomial if and only if $j\in\mathbb N_0$; in that case $v$ is a nonzero constant multiple of $L_j^{(2l+1)}$, and
$$u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)=c\,r^{l+1}e^{-kr}L_j^{(2l+1)}(2kr)\quad(c\ne0)$$
lies in $L^2(0,\infty;dr)$;

(e) *eigenfunction.* If $j\in\mathbb N_0$ then $u_{\mathrm{reg}}\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu_{\mathrm{reg}}=-k^2u_{\mathrm{reg}}$; equivalently, for every $m$ the transported function $\psi(r\Omega):=u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)Y_{lm}(\Omega)/r$ lies in $H^2(\mathbb R^3)\cap D(C)$ and satisfies $C\psi=-k^2\psi$.

The assertions are statements about the ordinary differential equation and
the operators $A_l,C$; no physical interpretation of $\gamma,k$ or of any
spectral level is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, let
$C:=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] (c) when $\gamma>0$, and the free Fourier multiplier when $\gamma=0$,
and let $U$ be the unitary of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-angular-radial-unitary-reduction]] from $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$
onto $K=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^2\bigl((0,\infty),dr\bigr)$, with coefficients
$u_{lm}=r\,c_{lm}$. For $l\ge0$ let $V_l$ be the closure of
$C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$ in $L^2(0,\infty;\mathbb C)$ for the norm
$$\|u\|_{V_l}^2:=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\Bigl|u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr|^2+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}|u(r)|^2+|u(r)|^2\Bigr)dr,$$
realized as the space of $u\in L^2$ with $u'-\frac ur\in L^2$ and
$\int|u|^2/r^2<\infty$ in the distributional sense
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and define
$$a_l(u,v):=\int_0^\infty\Bigl[\overline{\Bigl(v'(r)-\frac{v(r)}{r}\Bigr)}\Bigl(u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr)+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u(r)\overline{v(r)}-\frac{\gamma}{r}u(r)\overline{v(r)}\Bigr]dr .$$
Then:

(a) $V_l$ is a dense linear subspace of $L^2(0,\infty)$ that is a Hilbert space for $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$, the inclusion $V_l\hookrightarrow L^2(0,\infty)$ is continuous, and $a_l$ is a bounded symmetric sesquilinear form on $V_l$ that is closed and semibounded below;

(b) the operator $A_l$ defined by
$$D(A_l):=\Bigl\{u\in V_l:\exists\,f\in L^2(0,\infty)\ \text{with}\ a_l(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle\ \forall v\in V_l\Bigr\},\qquad A_lu:=f,$$
is well defined, self-adjoint and bounded below; $D(A_l)$ is dense in $V_l$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$ and $a_l(u,u)=\langle A_lu,u\rangle$ for $u\in D(A_l)$;

(c) for every $u\in D(A_l)$ the distributional identity $-u''+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)u=A_lu$ holds on $(0,\infty)$; consequently $u\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(0,\infty)$, $u$ is of class $C^1$ with $u'$ locally absolutely continuous, and the identity holds pointwise almost everywhere on $(0,\infty)$; if moreover $A_lu=Eu$ for some constant $E\in\mathbb C$ (in particular if $u$ is an eigenfunction of $A_l$), then $u$ is of class $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ and the differential equation holds pointwise there;

(d) *block identity.* For $\psi\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with $U\psi=(u_{lm})$ one has $\psi\in D(C)$ if and only if $u_{lm}\in D(A_l)$ for every $(l,m)$ and $\sum_{l,m}\bigl(\|u_{lm}\|^2+\|A_lu_{lm}\|^2\bigr)<\infty$; then $U(C\psi)=(A_lu_{lm})_{l,m}$. Equivalently $UCU^*=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}A_l$ on $K$;

(e) *eigenfunction transport.* If $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=Eu$ for some $E\in\mathbb R$, then the function $\psi(x):=u(r)Y_{l0}(\Omega)/r$ (with $x=r\Omega$) lies in $H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, satisfies $C\psi=E\psi$, and $r\mapsto u(r)/r$ is bounded on $(0,1]$; moreover $\psi$ is bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R^3$.

No endpoint boundary condition is imposed by hand: the domain $D(A_l)$ is the
form-domain realization transported from $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and no
physical interpretation of $A_l$, $C$, $U$ or $\gamma$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, let
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and let
$H_0:=-\Delta$ be the free operator of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
with domain $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]): $H_0=\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$
and $H_0u=-\Delta u$ for $u\in D(H_0)$, where $\Delta u$ is the distributional
Laplacian. Write $M$ for the multiplication operator
$$M u:=\frac{u}{|\cdot|},\qquad D(M):=\Bigl\{u\in H:\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\in H\Bigr\},$$
and write $\|u\|_2=\|u\|_H$. Then:

(a) for every $u\in D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ one has $u/|\cdot|\in L^2$ and

$$\Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le 2\sqrt{\|u\|_2\,\|\Delta u\|_2}\,,\qquad \Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le \eta\|\Delta u\|_2+\frac1\eta\|u\|_2\quad(\eta>0);$$

(b) $M$ is a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with $D(H_0)\subseteq D(M)$, symmetric on $D(H_0)$, with $H_0$-bound zero in the sense that for every $\eta>0$ the pair $(\eta,\eta^{-1})$ is admissible for $M$ relative to $H_0$;

(c) for every $\gamma>0$ the operator
$$C:=H_0-\gamma M,\qquad D(C):=D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C),$$
is self-adjoint on $H$, bounded below, and acts by $Cu=-\Delta u-\gamma u/|\cdot|$ for every $u\in D(C)$; for every $\eta\in(0,1/\gamma)$ one has $C\ge-\gamma\eta^{-1}/(1-\gamma\eta)$ in the quadratic-form sense.

No sharp lower bound of $C$ is claimed here, and no physical interpretation of
$C$, $H_0$, $\gamma$ or $\Delta$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, let
$H_0=-\Delta$ with $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the free operator
of [[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]],
let $M$ be the multiplier $Mu=u/|\cdot|$ of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]], and let
$$C:=H_0-\gamma M,\qquad D(C)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C),$$
be the self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] (c).
Write $\sigma_{\mathrm d}$, $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}$, $E$ for the discrete
spectrum, essential spectrum and spectral projection valued measure of
[[def-discrete-and-essential-spectrum-of-a-self-adjoint-operator]] and
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]. Then:

(a) $C$ is bounded below and $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C)=[0,+\infty)$;

(b) every point of $\sigma(C)\cap(-\infty,0)$ lies in $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(C)$: it is an eigenvalue of $C$ of finite multiplicity isolated in $\sigma(C)$, and the set of such eigenvalues is at most countable;

(c) the negative spectral subspace $E((-\infty,0))L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ is the closed linear span of the eigenspaces of $C$ for its negative eigenvalues.

No claim is made about the multiplicity or the number of the negative
eigenvalues, about the nonnegative part of the spectrum beyond
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C)=[0,\infty)$, or about any physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

derivations.claim: [The nonterminating tail] Suppose $j\notin\mathbb N_0$. Every $v_i$ is real and nonzero. Choose $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and an integer $I>\max(j,0)$ large enough that $(i-j)/(i+2l+2)\ge1-\varepsilon$ for all $i\ge I$. All coefficients from $I$ onward have one sign and $|v_{i+1}|\ge(1-\varepsilon)|v_i|/(i+1)$; induction gives $|v_i|\ge c(1-\varepsilon)^i/i!$ for $i\ge I$, where $c=|v_I|I!(1-\varepsilon)^{-I}>0$. Since the series is absolutely convergent, on $x\ge0$ the absolute value of its same-sign tail is its sum of absolute values. The reverse triangle inequality gives $|v(x)|\ge c e^{(1-\varepsilon)x}-P(x)$, where one may take the nonnegative polynomial $P(x)=\sum_{i<I}|v_i|x^i+c\sum_{i<I}(1-\varepsilon)^ix^i/i!$. Thus for sufficiently large $r$, $|u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)|\ge(c/2)r^{l+1}e^{k(1-2\varepsilon)r}$. Its squared integral diverges, since the exponent is positive; hence $u_{\mathrm{reg}}\notin L^2(0,\infty)$.

[Terminating solutions belong to the form domain] Suppose $j\in\mathbb N_0$ and write $u=r^{l+1}e^{-kr}v(2kr)$. Near zero, $u=O(r^{l+1})$, $u'=O(r^l)$ and $u/r=O(r^l)$; at infinity each decays exponentially times a polynomial. Therefore $u,u',u/r\in L^2$, and the trace at zero is zero. To verify $u\in V_l$ directly, choose a smooth cutoff $\chi_\delta$ that vanishes below $\delta$, equals one above $2\delta$ and has $|\chi_\delta'|\le C/\delta$. The additional derivative term obeys $\|\chi_\delta'u\|_2^2\le4C^2\int_\delta^{2\delta}|u/r|^2dr\to0$. The other omitted terms tend to zero by integrability; cutting off the exponential tail and then smoothing on compact subsets of $(0,\infty)$ gives compact smooth approximants in the $V_l$ norm. This is membership in the specified endpoint realization, rather than membership inferred from $L^2$ alone.

[The actual origin condition excludes the second solution] If $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=-k^2u$, then $u$ solves the classical radial equation by [F2]. By [F1] it is $c_1u_{\mathrm{reg}}+c_2u_2$. The regular quotient $u_{\mathrm{reg}}/r=O(r^l)$ is bounded, whereas $u_2/r\sim-r^{-l-1}/(2l+1)$. If $c_2\ne0$, the reverse triangle inequality therefore makes $|u(r)|/r\to\infty$, contrary to [F2]. Consequently $u=c_1u_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and every negative eigenspace has dimension at most one. Together with step 1.1 this proves (a).

[The form identity gives the operator domain and $H^2$ transport] The substitution of [F1] shows that $u$ solves $-u''+(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r)u=-k^2u$ on $(0,\infty)$. Against $w\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$, integration by parts gives $a_l(u,w)=\int(u'\overline{w'}+l(l+1)u\overline w/r^2-\gamma u\overline w/r)dr=-k^2\langle u,w\rangle$. The equality between the kinetic forms follows by integrating $(u\overline w/r)'$, with no boundary term because $w$ is compactly supported away from zero. Boundedness of $a_l$ and density in [F2] extend the identity to every $w\in V_l$. The actual definition of $D(A_l)$ now gives $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=-k^2u$. The vector with this one $(l,m)$ component belongs to the direct-sum graph domain, so the exact block identity gives $\psi=u(r)Y_{lm}(\Omega)/r\in D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ and $C\psi=-k^2\psi$ for every $m$. This argument uses no assertion that $e^{-k|x|}$ is smooth at $x=0$.

[All radial negative eigenvalues] Termination means $j=n-l-1\in\mathbb N_0$, so $n\ge l+1$ and $k=\gamma/(2n)$. Step 2.2 supplies a nonzero eigenvector at each $E_n=-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$, and step 2.1 shows its eigenspace is exactly $\mathbb Cu_{\mathrm{reg}}$. All other negative energies are excluded by steps 1.1 and 2.1. This proves (b), including every integer $n\ge l+1$, with no finite truncation of the bound family.

[All negative eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $C$] By the exact block/domain identity, $C\psi=E\psi$ is equivalent to $A_lu_{lm}=Eu_{lm}$ in every component, where $U\psi=(u_{lm})$. If $\psi\ne0$, at least one component is nonzero. Step 3.1 therefore forces $E=E_n$ for some $n\ge1$, and all components with $l\ge n$ vanish; the remaining finitely many components are scalar multiples of the regular solutions at $k=\gamma/(2n)$. Conversely each $E_n$ is a $C$ eigenvalue by taking the $l=m=0$ vector from step 2.2. Thus (c) and (d) hold. In fact every such eigenfunction is a finite linear combination of the transported regular solutions, which implies the asserted closed-span membership.

[Entire negative spectrum, including radial blocks] By [F3], every negative spectral point of $C$ is an eigenvalue, so step 4.1 proves $\sigma(C)\cap(-\infty,0)=\{E_n:n\ge1\}$. Fix $l$ and realize $A_l$ as the reducing $(l,0)$ block of $UCU^*$. If $\lambda<0$ is outside $\sigma(C)$, the restricted inverse of $C-\lambda$ supplies a bounded inverse for $A_l-\lambda$. If $\lambda=E_n$ with $n<l+1$, choose an open interval $J=(\lambda-\delta,\lambda+\delta)$ whose intersection with $\sigma(C)$ is just $\{\lambda\}$, as allowed by [F3]. The restricted projection on $J$ equals the restricted projection on $\{\lambda\}$ by [F4]; this is zero, since step 3.1 excludes a radial eigenvector at this energy. The restricted PVM is consequently supported outside $J$. Define $b(t)=(t-\lambda)^{-1}$ outside $J$ and $b(t)=0$ inside $J$. Both $b$ and $tb$ are bounded. By the exact-domain calculus [F4], its block multiplier maps into $D(A_l)$ and gives both $(A_l-\lambda)b(A_l)=I$ and $b(A_l)(A_l-\lambda)=I$ on the respective exact domains. Thus $\lambda\notin\sigma(A_l)$. The remaining negative points are eigenvalues from step 3.1, proving $\sigma(A_l)\cap(-\infty,0)=\{E_n:n\ge l+1\}$. This establishes the final exhaustion sentence for both operators, including absence of additional continuous negative radial spectrum.
[Conclusion] Step 2.1 proves (a), step 3.1 proves (b), step 4.1 proves (c) and (d), and step 5.1 proves the stated exhaustion of the entire negative spectra.
