Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$ and let
$C=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] with
essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$. For $n\ge1$, $0\le l\le n-1$ and
$-l\le m\le l$ let $u_{nl}$ be the regular solution of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-kummer-recurrence-and-termination]] at $k=\gamma/(2n)$
(the polynomial-exponential solution, unique up to a nonzero scalar), and put
$$\psi_{nlm}(x):=\frac{u_{nl}(r)}{r}Y_{lm}(\Omega)\qquad(x=r\Omega).$$
Then:

(a) each $\psi_{nlm}$ lies in $D(C)$ and $C\psi_{nlm}=-\frac{\gamma^2}{4n^2}\psi_{nlm}$; the vectors $\psi_{nlm}$ with distinct labels are pairwise orthogonal, and for fixed $n$ the eigenspace of $C$ at $-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$ is exactly their span; it has dimension $\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}(2l+1)=n^2$;

(b) after normalization, the family $(\psi_{nlm}/\|u_{nl}\|_2)_{n\ge1,0\le l\le n-1,-l\le m\le l}$ is a complete orthonormal family of the negative spectral subspace $E_C((-\infty,0))L^2(\mathbb R^3)$;

(c) the family is not complete in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$: the nonnegative spectral subspace $E_C([0,\infty))L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ is nonzero (indeed infinite dimensional), so the bound states alone do not span $L^2$.

All claims concern the mathematical spectral decomposition of $C$; no physical
interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, $l\ge0$,
$k>0$, let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]], write
$$j:=\frac{\gamma}{2k}-l-1,$$
and for $a=2l+1$ and $n\in\mathbb N_0$ let
$$L_n^{(a)}(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i\binom{n+a}{n-i}\frac{x^i}{i!}$$
be the $n$-th Laguerre polynomial of order $a$. Then:

(a) *substitution.* A $C^2$ function $u$ on $(0,\infty)$ satisfies $-u''+(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r)u=-k^2u$ if and only if $v(x):=e^{x/2}x^{-(l+1)}u(x/2k)$ is $C^2$ and satisfies $xv''+(2l+2-x)v'+jv=0$ on $(0,\infty)$;

(b) *regular series.* With $v_0:=1$ and
$$v_{i+1}:=\frac{(i-j)v_i}{(i+1)(i+2l+2)}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
the power series $v(x):=\sum_{i\ge0}v_ix^i$ converges for every $x\in\mathbb R$ and defines a solution of $xv''+(2l+2-x)v'+jv=0$ on $\mathbb R$;

(c) *regular solution and general solution.* The function
$$u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r):=r^{l+1}e^{-kr}v(2kr)$$
is a $C^\infty$ solution of the radial equation on $(0,\infty)$ with $u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)/r^{l+1}\to1$ as $r\downarrow0$; it is, up to a nonzero scalar multiple, the only solution with $u(r)/r^{l+1}$ bounded as $r\downarrow0$; every solution of the radial equation on $(0,\infty)$ is $c_1u_{\mathrm{reg}}+c_2u_2$ with $u_2$ defined near zero by $u_2(r):=u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)\int_{r_*}^r u_{\mathrm{reg}}(s)^{-2}ds$, where $0<r_*<\delta$ and $u_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has no zero in $(0,\delta)$, and extended uniquely to $(0,\infty)$ by the regular initial-value equation, and every solution that is not a multiple of $u_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has $|u(r)|/r$ unbounded as $r\downarrow0$;

(d) *termination.* $v$ is a polynomial if and only if $j\in\mathbb N_0$; in that case $v$ is a nonzero constant multiple of $L_j^{(2l+1)}$, and
$$u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)=c\,r^{l+1}e^{-kr}L_j^{(2l+1)}(2kr)\quad(c\ne0)$$
lies in $L^2(0,\infty;dr)$;

(e) *eigenfunction.* If $j\in\mathbb N_0$ then $u_{\mathrm{reg}}\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu_{\mathrm{reg}}=-k^2u_{\mathrm{reg}}$; equivalently, for every $m$ the transported function $\psi(r\Omega):=u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)Y_{lm}(\Omega)/r$ lies in $H^2(\mathbb R^3)\cap D(C)$ and satisfies $C\psi=-k^2\psi$.

The assertions are statements about the ordinary differential equation and
the operators $A_l,C$; no physical interpretation of $\gamma,k$ or of any
spectral level is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$, let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]), and let
$(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,\,-l\le m\le l}$ be the complete orthonormal family of
$L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]]. For pointwise formulas use the representatives $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]], and write $Y_{lm}(\Omega)$ for their values. Explicitly, with $P_l$ and $b_{lm}$ as in that supplier, for $0\le m\le l$,
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\Omega)=\frac{(-1)^m b_{lm}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}(\Omega_1+i\Omega_2)^m P_l^{(m)}(\Omega_3),\qquad \widetilde Y_{l,-m}=(-1)^m\overline{\widetilde Y_{lm}}\quad(1\le m\le l).$$
These are restrictions of polynomials in the Cartesian coordinates, hence smooth on the entire sphere, and represent the stated $L^2$ classes. Write
$L^2=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with Lebesgue measure and inner product linear
in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-hilbert-space]]), and let
$$K:=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^2\bigl((0,\infty),dr;\mathbb C\bigr)$$
be the Hilbert direct sum over $l\ge0$, $-l\le m\le l$. For $\psi\in L^2$ and
each $(l,m)$ define the coefficient function and the reduced function
$$c_{lm}(r):=\int_{S^2}\psi(r\Omega)\overline{Y_{lm}(\Omega)}\,d\sigma(\Omega)\quad(r>0,\ \text{a.e.}),\qquad u_{lm}(r):=r\,c_{lm}(r).$$
Then:

(a) for every $\psi\in L^2$ and every $(l,m)$ the function $u_{lm}$ is a well-defined element of $L^2((0,\infty),dr)$ depending only on the class of $\psi$, and $U\psi:=(u_{lm})_{l,m}$ is a linear isometry of $L^2$ into (indeed onto) $K$ with
$$\|U\psi\|_K^2=\sum_{l\ge0}\sum_{m=-l}^{l}\int_0^\infty|u_{lm}(r)|^2\,dr=\|\psi\|_{L^2}^2;$$

(b) $U$ is unitary, and for every $(u_{lm})\in K$ the finite-subset sums $\sum_{l\le N,\,|m|\le l}u_{lm}(r)Y_{lm}(\Omega)/r$ converge in $L^2$ to a function $\psi$ with $U\psi=(u_{lm})$;

(c) on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ every $f\in C^2$ satisfies the following identity. Here radial derivatives differentiate $F(r,\Omega)=f(r\Omega)$ with $\Omega$ fixed, and in angle coordinates $\Delta_{S^2}F:=\partial_\theta^2F+\cot\theta\,\partial_\theta F+\sin^{-2}\theta\,\partial_\varphi^2F$, extended continuously to the poles by the Cartesian identity proved below. For the smooth representatives of $Y_{lm}$ this agrees with the negative of the diagonal sphere operator in [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]]:

$$\Delta f=\partial_r^2f+\frac2r\partial_rf+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{S^2}f;$$

(d) for every $l\ge0$, $m$, and $u\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$, the function $\psi:=u(r)Y_{lm}(\Omega)/r$ lies in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\subseteq H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, its image under $U$ is the finite-support vector with $(l,m)$-entry $u$, and
$$-\Delta\psi=\frac1r\Bigl(-u''(r)+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u(r)\Bigr)Y_{lm}(\Omega),\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla\psi|^2\,dx=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\Bigl|u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr|^2+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}|u(r)|^2\Bigr)dr .$$

All statements are purely mathematical assertions about $L^2$ spaces, the
surface measure and the Laplacian; no physical interpretation and no statement
about operators with unbounded potentials is included.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Use the notation of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-harmonic-polynomial-dimension]]: $S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ with polar measure
$\sigma$ ([[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), the Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with inner
product linear in the first argument, the complete orthonormal family $(Y_{lm})$
([[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]],
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]]), the blocks $V_l=\operatorname{span}\{Y_{l,-l},\dots,Y_{ll}\}$ and
the finite span $H$, the spaces $H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ of complex harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$,
and the polynomial representatives $h_{lm}\in H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ of the $Y_{lm}$, characterized by
$\mathrm{res}_l(h_{lm})=Y_{lm}$ where $\mathrm{res}_l(p)$ is the class of $p|_{S^2}$
([[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]], [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]],
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). Put $H_{-1}^{\mathrm{pol}}:=\{0\}$, fix $l\ge0$ and $m\in\{-l,\dots,l\}$,
write $\mathcal H:=h_{lm}$, and define the three polynomial multipliers
$$Q_0:=x_3,\qquad Q_\pm:=\frac{x_1\pm ix_2}{\sqrt2},$$
so that $Q_q=\sum_{i=1}^3c_{q,i}x_i$ with $c_{0,i}=\delta_{i3}$ and $c_{\pm,i}=(\delta_{i1}\pm
i\,\delta_{i2})/\sqrt2$. Let $D_i$ and $L_z,L_3$ be as in
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-orbital-self-adjoint-generators]], where $L_3=L_z$ and $L_zY_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$
([[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]]). Then, for each $q\in\{-1,0,1\}$:

(a) (harmonic decomposition) the polynomial $G_q:=\dfrac{\sum_ic_{q,i}\,\partial_i\mathcal H}{2l+1}$ lies in
$H_{l-1}^{\mathrm{pol}}$ and
$$Q_q\,\mathcal H=R_q+r^2G_q,\qquad R_q:=Q_q\mathcal H-r^2G_q\in H_{l+1}^{\mathrm{pol}},$$
where $r^2(x)=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2$; for $l=0$ one has $G_q=0$ and $R_q=Q_q\mathcal H$;

(b) (degree selection) the function $Q_q|_{S^2}\cdot Y_{lm}$ lies in $V_{l+1}\oplus V_{l-1}$ (with
$V_{-1}:=\{0\}$); consequently, for all $l'\ge0$ and $m'\in\{-l',\dots,l'\}$,
$$\langle Q_q|_{S^2}\,Y_{lm},\ Y_{l'm'}\rangle=0\qquad\text{whenever } l'\notin\{l-1,\,l+1\};$$

(c) (weight selection) as elements of $H\subset L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ one has
$$L_z\bigl(Q_q|_{S^2}\,Y_{lm}\bigr)=\hbar(m+q)\,\bigl(Q_q|_{S^2}\,Y_{lm}\bigr),$$
because $\partial_\varphi Q_q=iq\,Q_q$ on $S^2$ ([[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]],
[[def-complex-exponential]]); hence in addition
$$\langle Q_q|_{S^2}\,Y_{lm},\ Y_{l'm'}\rangle=0\qquad\text{whenever } m'\ne m+q;$$

(d) (selection rules) combining (b) and (c): the angular matrix element
$\langle Y_{l'm'},\,Q_q|_{S^2}\,Y_{lm}\rangle$ can be nonzero only if
$$l'=l+1\ \text{and } m'=m+q,\qquad\text{or}\qquad l\ge1,\ l'=l-1\ \text{and } m'=m+q;$$
in particular only $\Delta l=\pm1$ and $\Delta m\in\{0,\pm1\}$ occur with the component-dependent shift
$\Delta m=q$ for the multiplier $Q_q$. These are necessary conditions on the angular integrals only: no
assertion is made that an allowed pair has a nonzero integral, and no absorption, emission or transition
probability is asserted or computed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $P_l$ be the Legendre polynomials of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-legendre-rodrigues-equation]], and for $l\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le m\le l$ define the
function $w_{lm}:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ by

$$w_{lm}(t):=(-1)^m(1-t^2)^{m/2}\,\frac{d^m}{dt^m}P_l(t),$$

where $(1-t^2)^{1/2}>0$ denotes the nonnegative square root. Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ and let the angle coordinates be $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$
([[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]],
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]). The image of $\Phi$ is
$S^2\setminus C$, where $C:=\{(x,0,z)\in S^2:x\ge0\}$; $C$ is closed and $\sigma(C)=0$ by applying the integral identity of
[[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]] to its indicator. For $l\ge m\ge0$, define the representative
$\widetilde Y_{lm}:S^2\to\mathbb C$ on $S^2\setminus C$ by
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)):=b_{lm}w_{lm}(\cos\theta)\frac{e^{im\varphi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},$$
and on the cut $C$ by
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta):=b_{lm}w_{lm}(\cos\theta)/\sqrt{2\pi}\qquad(0\le\theta\le\pi).$$
The limits at $\varphi=0$ and $2\pi$ agree because $m$ is an integer, and the endpoint values of $w_{lm}$ from (a) give the limits at the poles; hence $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ is continuous. For $1\le m\le l$ set
$\widetilde Y_{l,-m}:=(-1)^m\overline{\widetilde Y_{lm}}$, and write $Y_{lm}$ for the class of $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$. Then:

(a) each $w_{lm}$ extends continuously to $[-1,1]$, with $w_{lm}(\pm1)=0$ when $m\ge1$, and on $(-1,1)$
it satisfies the associated Legendre equation
$$-\bigl((1-t^2)w_{lm}'\bigr)'+\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}w_{lm}=l(l+1)w_{lm}\qquad(-1<t<1),$$
equivalently $(1-t^2)w_{lm}''-2tw_{lm}'+\Bigl[l(l+1)-\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}\Bigr]w_{lm}=0$;

(b) for fixed $m\ge0$ the functions $w_{lm}$, $l\ge m$, are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2((-1,1),dt)$:
$\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}w_{km}\,dt=0$ for $k\ne l$; moreover $0<\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt<+\infty$;

(c) with $b_{lm}:=\bigl(\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt\bigr)^{-1/2}>0$ and the representatives just defined, one has
$|Y_{l,-m}|=|Y_{lm}|$ and
$\overline{Y_{lm}}=(-1)^mY_{l,-m}$ for all $l$ and all $m$ with $|m|\le l$;

(d) the family $\{Y_{lm}:l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l\}$ is orthonormal in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]): for all $(l,m)\ne(l',m')$
with $|m|\le l$, $|m'|\le l'$, the integral $\int_{S^2}Y_{lm}\overline{Y_{l'm'}}\,d\sigma$ equals $0$, and it
equals $1$ when $(l,m)=(l',m')$;

(e) $w_{l0}=P_l$, and $w_{ll}(t)=(-1)^l\frac{(2l)!}{2^l l!}(1-t^2)^{l/2}$.

The functions $Y_{lm}$ are complex-valued $L^2$-functions on the sphere; no physical interpretation as angular
momentum eigenfunctions or spherical harmonics of an atom is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.
